title: Deadlocks and Concurrent Updates
learning_outcomes: Describe the purpose and main terms of Deadlocks and Concurrent Updates.
Use or interpret an appropriate PostgreSQL example connected to how deadlocks occur.
Identify one edge case and select a safe way to verify the expected result.

content.intro: This lesson focuses on Deadlocks and Concurrent Updates. Its primary job is to help you keep multi-step changes atomic and reason about snapshots, locks, waits, retries and competing transactions. The listed PDF subtopics define the coverage expected here; work through them in order and connect each one to an example, edge case and checkable result.
content.why_it_matters: This topic matters because PostgreSQL systems must preserve correct results as data grows and more sessions or services interact with it. Practicing deadlocks and concurrent updates teaches you to make assumptions explicit, apply the right SQL or operational tool, and verify behavior instead of relying on a demonstration that only worked once.

content_blocks.title: Core idea
content_blocks.text: Keep the problem small: keep multi-step changes atomic and reason about snapshots, locks, waits, retries and competing transactions. A PostgreSQL feature should be chosen for the semantics it provides, not just because it is available. Before executing a change, state the inputs, expected output and boundary conditions. The example below is intentionally small enough to inspect; it illustrates the idea but is not a substitute for a test against your schema and PostgreSQL version.

content_blocks.title: Worked example: Deadlocks and Concurrent Updates
content_blocks.code:
UPDATE products
SET price = price * 1.05
WHERE sku = 'SKU-100'
RETURNING sku, price;
content_blocks.expected_output: Returns the updated product row(s); zero rows means no SKU matched.
content_blocks.safety_note: UPDATE changes data; test inside a transaction and ROLLBACK before keeping changes.
content_blocks.run_instructions: Assumes a scratch products table with sku and numeric price. Review the WHERE clause before running.
content_blocks.reset_steps: For a read-only SELECT or inspection command, no reset is needed. For DDL/DML, use a disposable database; capture the starting state, run the example, inspect the result, and ROLLBACK or drop the lab objects as appropriate. Do not use production data or credentials.

task: Create a short practice artifact for “Deadlocks and Concurrent Updates”: explain its goal, show one example linked to “How deadlocks occur”, state the expected result, and include one edge/failure case and verification method. Use a disposable database or static artifact as appropriate.
hints: Start with the listed subtopics, especially “How deadlocks occur”, and describe the expected behavior in your own words.
Run or inspect the smallest example that demonstrates the behavior; do not add unrelated features before it is verified.
When the result surprises you, capture the exact SQL/error, check version and permissions, and change one assumption at a time.
expected_output: A reviewable note or query for Deadlocks and Concurrent Updates, with an explanation of “How deadlocks occur”, expected behavior, and a documented edge-case check.

common_mistakes.problem: Copying the example without checking its assumptions.
common_mistakes.why: Object names, data types, privileges, extensions and data distribution affect database behavior.
common_mistakes.fix: List schema/version assumptions and test with a tiny synthetic dataset first.

common_mistakes.problem: Treating a single successful query as proof of production readiness.
common_mistakes.why: A happy-path result does not test invalid input, concurrent sessions, permissions, recovery or query performance.
common_mistakes.fix: Add one negative/edge case and record the evidence that confirms the expected behavior.

common_mistakes.problem: Making a production change directly from a lesson.
common_mistakes.why: DDL, data updates, role changes and operational commands can affect data or availability.
common_mistakes.fix: Use an isolated lab, reviewed migration, least privilege, rollback/recovery plan and a second-person review for production.

summary: Deadlocks and Concurrent Updates fits into the broader goal to keep multi-step changes atomic and reason about snapshots, locks, waits, retries and competing transactions.
Use the curriculum subtopics as a completeness checklist: How deadlocks occur, Detecting deadlocks, Consistent lock ordering.
State the schema/version assumptions and verify one normal case plus an edge case before trusting the result.
